abstract: The paper introduces narrative-level streaming virality prediction as a new task for misinformation triage, motivated by the gap between the ~1.5-day peak virality of false narratives and the ~4.5-day median time for fact-checkers to publish corrections. The authors build an end-to-end streaming pipeline that clusters semantically equivalent posts into evolving narratives, detects anomalous cluster activity, normalizes claims via LLMs, and predicts remaining spread using a novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric, surfacing triage candidates before peak spread. Downstream components also advance the state of the art on claim normalization and check-worthiness detection, and the authors release the first dataset and baselines for this new task.
key_claims: The narrative cluster (a set of semantically equivalent claims), rather than individual posts or coarse events, is the natural unit of analysis for fact-checking workflows and virality prediction.
Automatic Claim Detection should extend beyond static classification to support pre-virality, claim-level streaming analysis aligned with how fact-checkers actually reason.
Task-specific prompting design matters more than raw model capacity for constrained claim normalization; a smaller Mistral-7B model beats larger models and prior state-of-the-art ensembles.
Early cluster-level virality dynamics are approximately linear, so regularized linear and kernel models match or outperform sequence models and point processes designed for cascade modeling.

A distilled, interpretable multi-task classifier outperforms a frontier LLM (Claude Opus 4.7) zero-shot on check-worthiness at far lower cost and latency, justifying modular distilled deployment over end-to-end frontier-LLM inference.
Decomposing check-worthiness into checkability, verifiability, and harm potential aligns model outputs with journalistic pre-judgment criteria and improves cross-dataset generalization.
methods: Constructed a dataset from the US Election 2020 Tweets corpus (Kaggle, Oct 15–Nov 08, 2020), yielding 1.52M tweets, with contiguous hourly bins and no-lookahead engagement snapshots.
Streaming clustering using paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings with incremental cosine-similarity clustering (threshold tuned to tau=0.65, O(n*k) time, bounded memory).

Online anomaly detection with EXPoSE (Expected Similarity Estimation via Random Kitchen Sinks / kernel density approximation), selected from the NAB benchmark, monitoring hourly tweet count and aggregate engagement.

LLM-based claim normalization using Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (and Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeek-3.1v) with two-stage retrieval verification (multilingual-e5-base embeddings), topic-aware retrieval, and contrastive few-shot prompting with negative demonstrations.

Virality prediction formulated as the Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR = (E_final - E_detect)/E_final), using 42 engineered features from a 6-hour post-detection window, evaluated across linear, tree, kernel, sequence, point-process (Hawkes), and text-based models on 529 clusters with 80/20 split.

Check-worthiness classification via a 4-Parallel-Heads DeBERTa-v3-large (full fine-tuning, 435M params) with a three-phase MTL schedule, auxiliary heads trained on soft labels from mistral-small-24b, evaluated on CheckThat! 2024, ClaimBuster, and CheckThat! 2023.
Frontier-LLM zero-shot ablation with Claude Opus 4.7 on CT24 test-gold (N=341); formative evaluation with six professional fact-checkers on 18 claim-report pairs.
findings: EXPoSE anomaly detection achieved NAB score 79.2, 97.9% detection rate before peak, and +23.0h median lead, dominating Bayesian changepoint, Etsy Skyline, and Steuber Z-score baselines.

Contrastive few-shot Mistral-7B (Approach 2) reached METEOR 0.5569 on the N=300 CT2025 English subset, exceeding the strongest published baseline (0.4569) by 10.0 METEOR points and beating larger models; fine-tuning underperformed prompting (0.4427).

On PSR prediction, BayesianRidge gave best ranking (rho=0.551) and SVR-RBF best fit (R2=0.336, MAE=0.207, F2@0.65=0.632); top simple models were statistically indistinguishable, while LSTM/GRU and Hawkes performed poorly.
User authority and temporal dynamics features dominated virality prediction while content features contributed minimally—who spreads a claim matters more than what it says for early-stage prediction.

The 4-Parallel-Heads classifier achieved F1=0.833 on CT2024 (vs prior SOTA 0.802), generalizing zero-shot to ClaimBuster (F1=0.973) and CheckThat! 2023 (F1=0.933); a late-fusion variant reached marginally higher CT2024 F1 (0.836) but generalized worse.
Claude Opus 4.7 zero-shot reached only F1=0.722 on CT24, trailing the distilled classifier by 0.11 F1 (McNemar p<10^-2) at ~$18/1k claims and ~9.9s latency vs <10ms.
86% of check-worthiness errors were shared across approaches, indicating representation learning rather than feature engineering is the bottleneck.

The pipeline surfaced ~500 fact-check candidates from ~1.5M posts over three weeks; the formative study showed 83.3% agreement (full agreement 50%) and all six fact-checkers rated the report structure as aligned with practice, with virality prediction rated least valuable.
contributions: A new task formulation: narrative-level streaming virality prediction, with an end-to-end pipeline integrating streaming clustering, online anomaly detection, claim normalization, and cluster-level spread prediction.
The novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric quantifying the remaining intervention window at detection time, distinguishing detection lead (~23h) from actionable triage lead (~17h).
State-of-the-art results on two established ACD tasks (CT2025 claim normalization and CheckThat! 2024 check-worthiness) using smaller/distilled models.
An interpretable 4-Parallel-Heads architecture decomposing check-worthiness into checkability, verifiability, and harm potential aligned with journalistic criteria.

The first public dataset and baselines for narrative-level streaming virality prediction (529 anomalous clusters, 535 claims, 42-feature inputs, virality and check-worthiness labels) from a 1.52M-post US political Twitter/X stream.
A frontier-LLM zero-shot ablation and a formative fact-checker study validating the cost-effectiveness and practical alignment of the modular design.
framing: The work sits at the intersection of virality prediction, claim normalization, check-worthiness detection, and explainable fact-checking, positioning itself against post-level and event-level virality work and static ACD classification. It is explicitly grounded in journalism research on fact-checkers' multi-stage cognitive decision process under time and attention constraints, arguing for pre-peak, narrative-centric, human-centered triage support.
